rows: Emergency Alerts is a UK government system for warning and advising people during life-threatening emergencies.
Alerts may be used for hazards such as wildfires, severe flooding and extreme storms.
Alerts are sent by emergency services or government bodies responsible for emergencies.
Compatible devices receive alerts through broadcasts from nearby mobile-phone masts.
The service works on UK 4G and 5G networks and does not require mobile data or Wi-Fi.
Users do not need to register, download an app or provide a phone number.
Recipients should stop and follow the instructions, but drivers must first find a safe and legal place to stop.
Emergency Alerts supplement rather than replace other warning channels such as radio, television and local communications.
An alert is based on the device's current area and does not prove a hazard at every property within that area.
Receipt depends on device compatibility, network connection, power state and broadcast coverage.
Vaccination is one measure that can reduce the risk of serious respiratory infection.
Bringing fresh air into indoor spaces can reduce the concentration of infectious respiratory particles.
Good hygiene, including covering coughs and cleaning hands, helps reduce spread.
Face coverings may be considered in crowded or enclosed settings and around people at higher risk.
UKHSA guidance covers flu, COVID-19 and other respiratory illnesses that commonly spread more in colder months.
People with symptoms should consider limiting contact with others, particularly those at higher risk of serious illness.
Respiratory infections can spread easily and can cause serious illness in some people.
Current advice should be checked because seasonal epidemiology and vaccination programmes can change.
General respiratory guidance does not establish an outbreak or infectious individual at a specific premises.
Local risk depends on current circulation, symptoms, ventilation, occupancy, vaccination and authorised outbreak evidence.
UKHSA guidance covers antiviral treatment of suspected or confirmed seasonal influenza.
The guidance also covers post-exposure antiviral prophylaxis.
Clinical recommendations include definitions and eligibility considerations.
Antiviral use requires consideration of pregnancy and breastfeeding.
Renal and hepatic function can affect antiviral selection or dosing.
The guidance was updated in January 2026 with additional renal-function dosing information.
Influenza is a respiratory infection that can spread easily and cause serious illness in some people.
General prevention measures such as vaccination, ventilation and hygiene remain relevant alongside clinical treatment.
Clinical antiviral guidance does not prove influenza transmission at a particular address.
Treatment and prophylaxis decisions require current clinical assessment, timing, exposure and patient-specific factors.
UKHSA guidance supports public-health management of hepatitis A infection.
The guidance aims to reduce secondary infections and prevent and control outbreaks.
The management guidance reviews the role of vaccine and human normal immunoglobulin for post-exposure prophylaxis.
The official resource includes a hepatitis A factsheet.
The resource includes contact, school and parent immunisation communication templates.
Oral-fluid testing instructions and request materials are provided for public-health use.
The collection was updated in February 2026 with revised and translated information resources.
General hepatitis A guidance does not establish a case, contact or contaminated source at a particular premises.
Case and outbreak conclusions require authorised clinical, laboratory, exposure and public-health investigation data.
